text: Something elusive is hard to find, hard to catch, or hard to pin down. It keeps staying just out of reach. The Burmese pythons here are elusive because they hide so well in the swamp that scientists gave up looking for the snakes and started testing the water for their DNA instead.

To simulate something is to set up a stand-in for a real situation on purpose, so you can study it or practise for it. The stand-in only has to match in the one way that matters. The scientists could not wait around for a real burglary, so after a pretend one they waited 30 minutes to copy the delay before real investigators would arrive. Flight simulators and fire drills work on the same idea.

To sift is to shake a mixture through a fine mesh so the small bits fall through and the lumps stay behind, the way bakers sift flour. It then grew into a second meaning: going through a big pile of anything to pull out the few parts you want. The researchers had vacuumed up ordinary house dust and had to sift it for the tiny bits of DNA inside.

A burglar breaks into a building in order to steal from it. That crime is called burglary, and it is not the same as robbery, which means taking something from a person by force or threat. Burglary usually happens when nobody is around, which is why investigators have to depend on whatever traces got left behind.

A housebreaker is another word for a burglar, someone who breaks into a house to steal. It sounds old-fashioned, and British writers still reach for it. Saying the news was better for housebreakers in Australia is a joke: their DNA was harder to catch there.

A crime scene is the place where a crime happened, treated as a source of evidence. Investigators seal it off and search it carefully, because anything moved, added or cleaned away can ruin what it might have told them. The crime scenes in this study were ordinary kitchens in houses a pretend burglar had just walked through.

A stray dog is one that has wandered off, and stray fibres are threads that have come loose and ended up where they do not belong. Used this way, stray means loose, scattered and unintended. Those fibres were not left on purpose; they simply fell off a burglar's clothes.

A fibre is a single thin thread, like one strand pulled from a sweater or a carpet. Americans spell it fiber; the British spelling used here is fibres. Investigators collect them because the fibres clinging to your clothes can be traced back to a particular fabric.

Something microscopic is far too small to see with your eyes alone. You need a microscope, which is where the word comes from. Microscopic strands of DNA are so small that a burglar has no way of knowing any were left behind.

A strand is one long thin piece of something, like a strand of hair or a strand of spaghetti. DNA gets described in strands because the molecule really is a long thin thread. One strand of it is nowhere near big enough to see.

Cautious means careful. Adding the prefix in- flips a word to its opposite, so incautious means careless, not taking enough care. To catch the incautious means to catch the burglars who were not careful enough. Writers sometimes use an adjective as a noun like this to mean the people who are that way.

Fragments are small pieces broken off something bigger, like the fragments of a smashed plate. The word tells you the pieces are incomplete. Fragments of genetic material means short broken bits of DNA rather than one whole molecule.

DNA is the long molecule inside almost every cell of a living thing that carries its building instructions, written as a sequence of four chemicals. The letters stand for deoxyribonucleic acid, which is why everybody just says DNA. Your sequence is the same in every one of your cells, and different enough from other people's that a tiny sample can be traced back to you.

Genetic means having to do with genes, the stretches of DNA that carry instructions passed from parents to their offspring. Genetic material is simply another way of saying DNA. The science of all this is called genetics.

A shed is a small building, but as a verb shed means to lose or drop something naturally, bit by bit, without trying. Dogs shed fur and trees shed leaves. This whole article rests on the fact that people shed tiny flakes of themselves everywhere they go.

A trace is an extremely small amount of something, left behind as a sign that it was there. Scientists talk about trace amounts constantly, meaning barely enough to detect. The traces here are specks of skin and spit far too small to notice.

Your body is built out of cells, tiny units of living material, and the ones making up the outer layer of your skin are skin cells. The outermost ones are already dead and flake off constantly, which is where much of household dust comes from. Each flake still holds a copy of your DNA.

Dandruff is the small white flakes of dead skin that come loose from the scalp and land on your shoulders. Everyone produces some of it. Because every flake carries your DNA, dandruff is one of the main things the air sampler picks up.

Saliva is the watery liquid your mouth makes, also called spit. It helps you taste food and begin digesting it. Tiny droplets of saliva leave your mouth whenever you talk, laugh or cough, and your DNA goes with them.

Being suspended from school means being kept out of it for a while, but in science suspended means floating in a liquid or a gas instead of settling. Dust suspended in air is held up in it, not lying on the floor. That is the state the DNA has to be in for a vacuum to catch it.

Debris is scattered broken pieces or rubbish left behind after something falls apart, as in storm debris or space debris. The word came from French, so the final s is silent and it sounds like duh-BREE. A personal debris cloud means the drifting bits of skin and spit hanging around a person.

To hang around is to stay somewhere a while without doing much, and the phrase also covers things that linger instead of clearing away. A smell can hang around a room for hours. This debris cloud hangs around for at least half an hour after the person has gone.

A journal can be a diary you write in, but in science a journal is a magazine where researchers publish studies so other scientists can read and check them. Each one covers a field, and this study appeared in Forensic Science International: Genetics. Saying a study was published in a journal tells you other experts looked it over first.

A volunteer usually means someone who helps out without being paid. In research it means a person who agrees to take part in a study. Two sets of volunteers appear here: the 22 households that let the team in, and the people who played the burglar.

To ransack a place is to search roughly right through it, pulling things out and leaving a mess, usually hunting for something to steal. The word suits a burglar rather than a careful searcher. These volunteers only pretended to ransack the houses, opening drawers and cupboards for 15 minutes.

A controlled test is an experiment the researchers set up themselves, so they decide exactly what happens and already know the right answer. That is how you find out whether a method works. Here the scientists knew which person had walked through each house, so they could check whether the air gave the same answer.

Scarpered is British slang for ran off quickly, especially to get away. An American writer would say bolted or took off. It is a light, almost joking word, which is why it fits a pretend burglary better than a real one.

Forensic science is science used to answer questions for courts and criminal investigations: fingerprints, DNA, bloodstains, bullet marks. People shorten it to forensics, and a forensics team is the group that collects and tests the evidence. The word traces back to a Latin word for the public square where legal cases were argued.

Awkward can mean clumsy, but here it means uncomfortable and hard to deal with. An awkward question is one you would rather not have to answer. Your DNA turning up in a stranger's kitchen is not proof you robbed it, but it is awkward.

To carry out a plan, an order or a study is to do it, to put it into action. It is one of the commonest phrases in writing about research. Carried out by a team led by Chiara Fantinato just means her team did the study.

Chiara Fantinato is the scientist at Oslo University Hospital in Norway who led this study. The article later calls her Dr Fantinato, because she holds a doctorate. She is the one who described their air sampler as basically a vacuum cleaner.

Oslo is the capital and largest city of Norway, in northern Europe. The research team is based at a hospital there, and half of the 22 test houses were in the city. Air samples in Oslo matched the intruder 82 percent of the time.

An application can be a form you fill in or a program on a phone, but here it means a use, a way of putting something to work. Calling the study an impressive application of these methods means the scientists found a clever new use for them. Anything that can be put to work has applications.

To analyse something is to examine it closely, breaking it into parts to work out what it is made of or what it means. Americans spell it analyze; the British spelling used here is analyse. The team analysed the dust to find out whose DNA was in it.

Environmental DNA, shortened to eDNA, is the DNA a living thing leaves behind in its surroundings: in water, in soil, or in air. Instead of finding the creature, you test the place and work out who passed through. Ecologists have used it for more than 20 years, and this study points it at burglars.

An organism is any individual living thing: a bacterium, a mushroom, an oak tree, a snake, a person. Biologists use it when they need one word that covers all of them. Every organism sheds DNA into its surroundings.

Ecologists are scientists who study living things and how they interact with each other and with their surroundings. Working out which animals live in a lake or a forest is exactly their kind of question. They invented the eDNA trick long before anyone aimed it at a crime scene.

A party can have a good atmosphere, but the scientific meaning is the layer of gases surrounding a planet. On Earth, that is the air. Taking eDNA from water, soil and atmosphere means collecting it from all three, air included.

A technique is a particular way of doing something, usually one that takes skill and has been worked out carefully. A swimming stroke and a laboratory procedure are both techniques. The technique here is capturing DNA out of the air and reading it.

Burmese pythons are enormous snakes from South East Asia that people kept as pets in Florida and then let loose. They now breed in the wild there and eat native animals, which makes them an invasive species. They hide so well in the swamp that scientists look for their DNA in the water rather than for the snakes.

The Everglades are a huge area of shallow water, sawgrass and swamp covering much of southern Florida, a large part of it national park. It is wet, dense and enormous. Finding one particular animal in it by looking is close to hopeless, which is why eDNA helps.

An audit is an official check of records or numbers, usually to see whether the money adds up. Said of Loch Ness, to audit the inhabitants means to take a careful official count of everything living in it. The joke is that counting lake creatures gets the same solemn treatment as counting a company's cash.
The inhabitants of a place are the ones who live there. It works for people in a country and for animals in a lake. Testing the water told scientists which creatures inhabited Loch Ness.

Loch Ness is a long, very deep lake in Scotland; loch is the Scottish word for lake. It is famous for the Loch Ness monster, which people have claimed to see for almost a century. When scientists tested its water for DNA they found fish and a great many eels, and nothing monstrous.

Plesiosaurs were large sea reptiles with long necks and four paddle-shaped flippers. They lived at the same time as the dinosaurs and died out with them. A plesiosaur is what the Loch Ness monster is usually drawn to look like, so no plesiosaurs is the writer's way of reporting that the DNA found no monster.

A profile can be your page on an app or the outline of a face seen from the side, but it also means a short set of key facts describing someone. A genetic profile is a set of measurements taken at known spots along a person's DNA. Two profiles can be laid side by side to see whether two samples came from the same person.

The occupants of a space are the people in it at the time. A room that is occupied has somebody using it. The Oslo team could build DNA profiles of a room's occupants out of its air, even after everyone had left.

Adelaide is a city on the southern coast of Australia and the capital of the state of South Australia. The other 11 test houses were there. Air samples in Adelaide matched the intruder only 36 percent of the time, and nobody is sure why.

To mock someone is to make fun of them, but as a describing word mock means fake, done for practice or pretence. A mock exam and a mock trial are rehearsals for the real thing. A mock burglar is a volunteer pretending to burgle a house.

Gear is an everyday word for the equipment an activity needs, like football gear. Protective gear is clothing worn to keep something safe: suits, gloves, masks, goggles. This team wore it not to protect themselves but to keep their own DNA out of the house.

An intruder is someone who comes into a place without being allowed or wanted. The word says nothing about stealing, only about not belonging there. The intruders in this study were volunteers who had never visited the houses before.

A cupboard is a cabinet with a door and shelves for storing things. British writers say cupboards where Americans would usually say cabinets or closets. Opening drawers and cupboards is what a burglar does while hunting for valuables.

To flee is to run away from danger, and fled is its past form. Fled the scene is a set phrase out of news and police reports, meaning left the place quickly after something happened. Nothing bad actually happened here, so the writer is borrowing the crime-report tone on purpose.

To contribute is to give something toward a larger whole, often money or help. It also works for anything that becomes part of something bigger. Airborne DNA settles on the floor and contributes to surface dust, meaning it becomes part of it.

You sweep a floor with a broom, and as a noun here a sweep is a sample gathered by wiping across a surface. Forensic teams take sweeps of a shelf or a windowsill to collect whatever has settled there. The researchers took sweeps as well as air, because airborne DNA eventually lands.

Whereas is a formal joining word meaning while, by contrast. It sets two facts side by side to point out how different they are. Whereas Oslo matched 82 percent of the time, Adelaide managed only 36 percent.

In maths, factors are numbers that multiply together, but in ordinary writing a factor is any one thing that helps cause a result. Listing the factors behind a bad test score you might say tiredness, noise and not studying. The factors suggested here include the weather indoors, how many people live in the house, and how recently the rooms were cleaned.

You stir soup with a spoon, and to stir something up is to set it moving and mixing. Walking across a room stirs settled dust back up into the air. That is a real problem for this method, because old DNA can rise again and look new.

To set foot in a place is to enter it at all, even for a second. The phrase nearly always turns up with a negative, as in never set foot inside. People who have never set foot inside a house can still leave DNA there, carried in on somebody else's clothes.

A sensitive person is easily upset, but a sensitive instrument or method is one that can detect very small amounts of something. The more sensitive it is, the fainter the signal it can pick up. This technique was so sensitive that it caught the researchers' own DNA straight through their protective suits.

A pipe leaks when liquid escapes through a gap, and the word covers anything that gets out where it should not, including secrets and information. DNA leaking into the crime scenes means their own DNA getting in by accident. Nothing was actually dripping.

A sample is a small amount collected so that it can stand for the whole of something: a blood sample, a water sample. You test the sample instead of testing everything. An air sample from one kitchen is meant to represent whatever was floating through that room.

To clinch something is to settle it for certain, the way a last-minute goal clinches a win. Clinching evidence is the piece that decides a case on its own. Dr Fantinato says air samples will probably never be that.

Guilt can mean the bad feeling you get after doing something wrong, but in law it means actually having committed the crime. A court decides guilt whatever the person happens to feel. Evidence of someone's guilt is evidence that they did it.

An investigation is an organised search for the truth about something, and an investigative tool is anything that helps with one. Calling air DNA a tool rather than proof is a careful choice of words. It can point investigators toward a person; it cannot convict them.

Calling something part of the puzzle means it is one piece of information among several, useful only alongside the rest. The picture behind it is a jigsaw: one piece does not show you much. Dr Fantinato uses it to say air DNA has to be combined with other evidence.

A nuance is a small difference or fine detail that matters once you look closely. Understanding the nuances of something means getting past the rough version to the particulars. The nuances here include why one person sheds far more DNA than another.

To standardise something is to make everyone do it the same agreed way, so that results from different places can be compared. Screw sizes and school tests are standardised. Until labs standardise these techniques, two labs could test the same air and report different things. Americans spell it standardizing.

An enquiry is a question or an investigation; Americans spell it inquiry. Helping police with their enquiries is a famous British phrase that sounds polite but usually means somebody is being questioned as a suspect. Ending on it is a joke: the team wants to help the police, and their method would put burglars in exactly that position.
